evals.prompt: Turn these notes into a 1,000-word engineering launch post: our dashboard used to poll every 15 seconds; we replaced it with a WebSocket event stream and a reconnecting client state machine; median update delay fell from 8.2s to 410ms; duplicate events during reconnect were the main rollout issue. Audience: technical customers. Do not invent other numbers.
evals.expected_output: A causal engineering narrative with a specific title, action-led headings, an explanation of the old constraint, the architecture change, the reconnect tradeoff, and the measured result.

evals.prompt: Write a technical blog draft explaining how we stopped a background document-indexing queue from delaying interactive search. Facts: both workloads shared the same worker pool; indexing saturated the queue at peak; we split interactive and batch paths, added per-tenant concurrency limits, and shadow-tested the new routing for two weeks. We have no final latency numbers yet.
evals.expected_output: A credible technical draft that does not invent metrics, centers the live-versus-batch path conflict, and uses an honest placeholder only if a metric is materially needed.

evals.prompt: Write a 500-word post for developers about moving API authorization from a gateway plugin into the service layer. The real benefit was consistent policy evaluation for HTTP, WebSocket, and async job entry points. Keep the tone calm and practical; no claims about security improvements beyond that consistency.
evals.expected_output: A short engineering explainer with a compact causal arc, no speculative security claims, and a conclusion that connects the architectural boundary to consistent behavior.
